name: Horizontal gaze pathway
summary: Looking to the left requires the left lateral rectus and the right medial rectus to contract together. The command starts in the right frontal eye field (for voluntary saccades) or the parieto-occipital cortex (for pursuit), descends to the left paramedian pontine reticular formation, which fires the left abducens nucleus; that nucleus contains both the motor neurons for the left lateral rectus and the interneurons whose axons cross and ascend in the right MLF to the right medial rectus subnucleus of the oculomotor nucleus. Lesions of the frontal eye field, the PPRF, the abducens nucleus and the MLF each produce a characteriztic and localizable pattern.

origin.note: Frontal eye field (saccades) and parieto-temporo-occipital cortex (pursuit); also the superior colliculus and vestibular nuclei.

neuronChain.synapse: contralateral PPRF (directly and via the superior colliculus)
contralateral oculomotor nucleus (medial rectus subnucleus) via the MLF

decussation.level: Cortex to PPRF (crossed in the midbrain–pons) and abducens interneurons to the contralateral MLF
decussation.note: Double crossing: the cortex drives the contralateral PPRF, whose abducens nucleus drives the contralateral medial rectus through the MLF.

waypoints.note: motor neurons to the lateral rectus; interneurons to the MLF
interneuron axons cross and ascend in the MLF

termination: Lateral rectus (abducens nerve) of one eye and medial rectus (oculomotor nerve) of the other.

lesionEffectsByLevel.effects: Eyes deviate toward the lesion; cannot look voluntarily to the opposite side; vestibulo-ocular reflex intact; recovers in days
Eyes and head turn away from the focus
Loss of ipsilateral saccades; eyes deviate away from the lesion; oculocephalic reflex can still bring the eyes across
Complete ipsilateral gaze palsy not overcome by the oculocephalic reflex, usually with an ipsilateral facial palsy
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: the ipsilateral eye fails to adduct, the contralateral eye shows abducting nystagmus, convergence spared
One-and-a-half syndrome: only abduction of the contralateral eye survives

pearls: Hemisphere: eyes look toward the lesion. Pons: eyes look away from the lesion
A gaze palsy that head turning overcomes is supranuclear; one it cannot overcome is nuclear
INO is the MLF; bilateral INO in a young adult is multiple sclerosis
